outline.chapter_title: Framing the Doctrine: Proving Patent Infringement and Standards of Review
outline.description: Introduces the substantive and procedural foundations that govern jury trials and appellate review in patent cases, with an emphasis on the evidentiary burdens and Rule 50 (JMOL) posture that structure the Finesse Wireless appeal.
subtopics: Elements of patent infringement and the all-elements rule
Burden of proof: preponderance of the evidence on infringement
Jury role versus judge role in patent trials
JMOL under Rule 50(a)/(b): timing, preservation, and grounds
Regional-circuit standard for reviewing denial of JMOL (Fifth Circuit "overwhelming evidence" formulation)
Federal Circuit standards: substantial-evidence review of jury findings; de novo review of claim construction

outline.chapter_title: Technical Primer: Intermodulation Products, PIM, and DSP Concepts
outline.description: Builds a working vocabulary for the radio-frequency and digital-signal-processing concepts essential to understanding the patents and the infringement theories at issue.
subtopics: Intermodulation products (IMPs) and passive intermodulation (PIM): internal vs. external sources
Transmit/receive paths, co-located transmitter and receiver architectures
Oversampling and decimation; creating and filtering bit streams
Phase and amplitude adjustment; sub-sample phase shifts
Model-based PIM cancellation (PIM-C) features in commercial radios
Multiplication of signals in DSP: baseband/complex representations, modulus (|x|), complex conjugate (x′)

outline.chapter_title: How to Prove Infringement of Method Claims
outline.description: Explains what plaintiffs must show to establish that an accused device or user performs each step of a claimed method, emphasizing temporal ordering and evidentiary mapping.
subtopics: Method claims: proving performance of each step and the sequence of operations
Using design documents, source code, and testing as proof of performance
Linking technical blocks to claim limitations: receivers, ADCs, filters, multipliers
Temporal feasibility: a step cannot operate on a signal that does not yet exist
Direct infringement by users of vendor features (e.g., carriers using PIM-C in supplied radios)
Common pitfalls: ambiguity in what constitutes a "signal" versus a transform of a signal

outline.description: Outlines the methodology for construing claim language and the associated standards of review, then situates the disputed terms from the case within that framework.
subtopics: Intrinsic evidence hierarchy: claim language, specification, prosecution history
Extrinsic evidence: expert and inventor testimony as context, not control
Standard of review: de novo construction; clear-error review of subsidiary facts
Construing "three signals S1, S2, S3": separately identifiable vs. unique
Other contested terms not reached on appeal (e.g., "receiver," "co-located"): why appellate courts sometimes bypass them
Impact of constructions on evidentiary burdens at trial

outline.description: Explores when statements or amendments during prosecution limit claim scope, and how courts discern clear and unambiguous disclaimers.
subtopics: Doctrinal test: clear and unmistakable disavowal required to narrow claim scope
Amendments for patentability and their interpretive consequences
Finesse’s amendment from "two or three signals" to "three signals": what it did and did not concede
Distinguishing subject-matter scope from input-signal uniqueness
Continental Circuits v. Intel and related authority on disavowal
Strategic drafting and response practices to avoid unintended narrowing

outline.chapter_title: Case Study Setup: Finesse Wireless v. AT&T & Nokia
outline.description: Presents the parties, patents, asserted claims, trial verdict, and the issues preserved for appeal to situate the opinion within the litigation timeline.
subtopics: The patents-in-suit: ’134 (sampling and cancellation pipeline) and ’775 (seven multiplications of three signals)
Accused functionality: Nokia’s PIM-C feature used in AT&T’s network
Jury verdict: liability and lump-sum damages award
Post-trial motions: JMOLs and motion for new trial
Appellate issues: noninfringement JMOL, damages/new trial, and constructions not reached
Jurisdictional path to the Federal Circuit

outline.chapter_title: Teaching the ’134 Patent: Sampling the Passband and Identifying the Claimed Signals
outline.description: Uses the ’134 patent dispute to develop doctrine on evidentiary mapping of claim limitations, especially where timing and signal identity are dispositive.
subtopics: Claim 1(a): oversampling a passband that includes both "signals of interest" and "interference generating signals"
Core factual dispute: whether the RF ADC samples the interference-generating signals
Expert mapping reliance on a vendor legend: DL(TX) reference vs. modeled PIM path
Temporal impossibility: modeled PIM path generated downstream of the RF ADC
The attempted pivot to x1/x2: ambiguity and contradictions in expert testimony
Johns Hopkins v. Datascope: why self-contradictory expert opinions cannot support a verdict
Substantial-evidence application: when the record compels JMOL for noninfringement

outline.chapter_title: Teaching the ’775 Patent: "Three Signals" and the "Seven Multiplications" Requirement
outline.description: Develops the evidentiary and doctrinal lessons from the ’775 patent on satisfying multi-part mathematical-operation limitations and the role of claim construction and disavowal.
subtopics: Construction of S1, S2, S3: separately identifiable signals need not be unique
Prosecution history did not clearly disavow two unique inputs plus a copy
Limitation 1(d): proving seven third-order multiplications are actually performed
Distinguishing multiplications from operations on modulus and complex conjugates
Why identifying only three distinct multiplications is insufficient
The necessity of a faithful mapping from accused operations to all seven claimed products
Substantial-evidence analysis: the insufficiency of post-hoc mapping not presented to the jury

outline.chapter_title: Appellate Disposition and Remedies: JMOL Reversal and Damages Vacatur
outline.description: Explains the Federal Circuit’s ultimate rulings, including its reliance on substantial-evidence principles and the routine vacatur of damages when liability falls.
subtopics: Reversal of denial of JMOL for both patents based on lack of substantial evidence
Damages award vacated as a consequence of noninfringement
Standard and posture for new-trial motions on damages (Fifth Circuit abuse-of-discretion review)
Unreached issues: claim construction disputes and their mootness
Allocation of costs on appeal

outline.chapter_title: Litigation Strategy Lessons: Building and Defending Complex Technical Infringement Cases
outline.description: Extracts practical guidance for trial lawyers and experts in proving (or rebutting) infringement in technology-heavy cases.
subtopics: Prepare precise, consistent expert mappings of every claim element to concrete accused operations
Avoid reliance on ambiguous vendor legends; corroborate with timing diagrams and source code
Explain temporal sequencing to show feasibility (or impossibility) of steps like sampling
Account for mathematical transforms (|x|, x′) and justify why they qualify as the claimed "signals"
Use demonstratives that enumerate and align all required operations (e.g., seven multiplications)
Preserve arguments at Rule 50(a) to avoid waiver; build the record with pinpoint citations
Cross-examination strategies: exposing contradictions and unperformed steps

outline.chapter_title: Comparative Case Law: Substantial Evidence and Expert Testimony in the Federal Circuit
outline.description: Situates the opinion alongside other key decisions addressing sufficiency of evidence, expert coherence, and mapping requirements in patent cases.
subtopics: Apple v. Wi-LAN: substantial evidence review of infringement and damages
Wi-LAN v. Apple: regional-circuit JMOL standards and Federal Circuit deference
Johns Hopkins v. Datascope: effect of contradictory expert testimony
Continental Circuits v. Intel: disavowal/disclaimer standards and scope control
Themes: the all-elements rule, evidentiary precision, and the dangers of post-hoc rationalization
Patterns in reversals arising from missing or speculative element-by-element proof

outline.chapter_title: Implications for Patent Drafting, Prosecution, and Product Design
outline.description: Explores how the opinion informs prospective patent strategy and engineering design choices, especially where signal identity and mathematical operations are central.
subtopics: Claiming "signals" versus "functions of signals": drafting to reduce ambiguity
Enumerating operations (e.g., seven multiplications) and providing alternative formulations
Prosecution responses that preserve breadth while distinguishing prior art
Design-around opportunities: restructuring DSP pipelines, ordering of operations, and transforms
Evidentiary preparedness: creating documentation that accurately reflects signal paths and timing
Risk management in venues with high patent dockets (e.g., E.D. Tex.)

outline.description: Provides exercises and hypotheticals to reinforce doctrinal learning and to practice applying the opinion’s reasoning to new facts.
subtopics: Problem: Can |x2| or x2′ count as S3 where the claim recites "three signals"? Explain your mapping and limits.
Problem: An accused radio computes ten third-order terms. How would you prove which seven satisfy the claim?
Problem: The ADC samples x1 and x2; a PIM model is computed later. Can plaintiff still meet ’134 claim 1(a)?
Problem: Draft cross-exam questions to test whether seven distinct multiplications are performed
Short answer: What record showing would avoid the "self-contradictory expert" problem?
Checklist: Building an element-by-element mapping for math-heavy method claims
